{{Short description|Serpent-like curve}}
{{about|the mathematical concept|the design feature|Serpentine shape}}
A '''serpentine curve''' is a curve whose Cartesian equation is of the form<ref>{{Cite web |title=Serpentine |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Curves/Serpentine/ |access-date=2025-09-20 |website=Maths History |language=en}}</ref>
:<math>x^2y+a^2y-abx=0, \quad ab > 0</math>

Its functional representation is
:<math>y = \frac{abx}{x^2 + a^2}</math>

Its [[Parametric equation|parametric equation]] for <math>0 < t < \pi</math> is
:<math>x=a\cot(t)</math>
:<math>y=b\sin(t)\cos(t)</math>

Its parametric equation for <math> -\pi / 2 < t < \pi / 2 </math> is<ref name="mathworld">{{cite web |last1=Weisstein |first1=Eric |title=Serpentine Curve |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SerpentineCurve.html |website=Wolfram MathWorld |access-date=20 September 2025}}</ref>
:<math>x=a\tan(t)</math>
:<math>y=b\sin(t)\cos(t)</math>


It has a maximum at <math>x = a</math> and a minimum at <math>x = -a</math>, given that
:<math>y' = \frac{ab\left(a-x\right)\left(a-x\right)}{\left(a^2+x^2\right)^2} = 0</math>
The minimum and maximum points are at <math> \pm b / 2 </math>, which are independent of <math> a </math>.


The inflection points are at <math> x = \pm \sqrt{3}a </math>, given that
:<math>y'' = \frac{2abx\left(x^2 - 3a^2\right)}{\left(x^2+a^2\right)^3} = 0 </math>


In the parametric representation, its curvature is given by<ref name="mathworld" />
:<math>\kappa(t) = -\frac{2ab \cot t \left(\cot^2 t - 3\right)}{\left(b^2 \cos^2 \left(2t\right) + a^2 \csc^4 4\right)^{3/2}}</math>

An alternate parametric representation:<ref>{{cite web |last1=Weisstein |first1=Eric |title=Serpentine Curve |url=https://archive.lib.msu.edu/crcmath/math/math/s/s215.htm |access-date=20 September 2025}}</ref>
:<math>\kappa(t) = \frac{2abx\left(x^2 - 3a^2 \right)}{\left(x^2 + a^2 \right)^3 \left(1 + \frac{\left(a^3 b - abx^2\right)^2}{\left(x^2 + a^2\right)^4}\right)^{3/2}}</math>


A generalization of the curve is given by the [[Flipped Curve|flipped curve]] when <math>a = 2</math>, resulting in the flipped curve equation<ref>{{cite web |title=flipped curve |url=https://2dcurves.com/higher/higherf.html |website=2dcurves |access-date=20 September 2025}}</ref>
:<math>y^2\left(x^2+1\right)^2 = x^2</math>
which is equivalent to a serpentine curve with the parameters <math>a = 1, b = \pm1</math>.

==History==

[[Guillaume de l'Hôpital|L'Hôpital]] and [[Christiaan Huygens|Huygens]] had studied the curve in 1692, which was then named by [[Isaac Newton|Newton]] and classified as a [[Cubic plane curve|cubic curve]] in 1701.<ref name="mathworld" />
